title: Security & Compliance Operational Playbook: RBAC, Audit, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence, Risk
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook defines Redwood Inference's operational controls and workflows for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) controls, incident response for security events, compliance evidence collection and retention, and the formal risk & exceptions process. The guidance below is intended for engineering, security, and compliance owners who operate or onboard services and customers.

Scope
Applies to: all Redwood-managed control plane services, hosted inference endpoints, Dedicated and Private deployment integrations, administrative consoles, and developer tooling. Customer-specific contractual variations (e.g., bespoke data residency obligations) are noted where applicable.

Executive summary
- RBAC: Principle of least privilege with role-review cadence, automated role-binding checks, and central identity provider (IdP) integration.
- Audit logging: Immutable, centralized audit stream with minimum retention baselines and tiered retention by sensitivity.
- Data residency & retention: Region-aware storage buckets and retention policy engine per dataset class.
- Secure SDLC: Gate checks (SCA, secrets scanning), signed releases, and mandatory threat modeling for sensitive changes.
- Incident response (security): Playbooks for triage, containment, forensic capture, customer communication and post-incident evidence.
- Compliance evidence: Automated evidence ingestion into the compliance evidence store with owner, retention, and attestation workflows.
- Risk & exceptions: Formal request, technical justification, approval matrix, and time-boxed exceptions with compensating controls.

1) Roles and responsibilities
- Security: policy owner, final approver for exceptions, incident cmd support.
- Engineering (service owners): implement RBAC, generate evidence artifacts, perform runbook validation.
- Platform/Infra: maintain audit pipeline, retention tooling, KMS/HSM integrations.
- Compliance/Legal: verify evidence completeness for audits and customer contracts.

2) RBAC & Authentication

Principles
- Principle of least privilege (PoLP).
- Role-based assignments, not user-level long-lived access keys.
- Centralized identity provider (Okta / Azure AD) with SCIM provisioning for groups.
- Require MFA for all interactive admin access.

Role matrix (summary)
- roles: Reader, Data-Analyst, Service-Operator, Service-Admin, Platform-Operator, Security-Admin, Compliance-Auditor.
- Example bindings:   - Service-Admin: full control over a single microservice (create/rollback/deploy).   - Platform-Operator: cluster-level ops (scale/pool changes) but not customer data export.   - Compliance-Auditor: read-only access to audit logs and evidence store.

RBAC lifecycle and review process

1. Ownership: every role binding must have an owner (team + oncall alias).
2. Quarterly review: role & group membership report generated by infra and emailed to owners.
3. Automated alerts: membership changes trigger Slack notifications and an audit event.
4. De-provisioning: onboarding/offboarding runs via HR to IdP sync (max 72 hours for full removal).

Authentication requirements
- SSO via SAML/OIDC.
- Enforce FIDO2 or TOTP MFA for admin tiers.
- Short-lived service credentials (<= 12 hours) for service-to-service tokens using internal token broker.
- No embedded long-lived secrets in source control.

RBAC examples (policy snippets)
- Example service role (pseudo-JSON):
  {
    "role": "service-admin",
    "permissions": ["deploy","rollback","view-metrics"],
    "scope": "service:payments"
  }

3) Audit logging

Objectives
- Provide a tamper-evident, searchable audit trail for security-sensitive events: auth events, role changes, privilege escalations, API key creation, customer data exports, admin console actions, and deployment rollbacks.

Architecture and retention
- Ingest: agents forward logs to a centralized Kafka ingestion cluster.
- Processing: logs enriched and written to an append-only audit index (immutable write path) and backed up to object storage.
- Access: read-only queries through the audit UI; evidence exports require Compliance-Auditor role plus 2FA.

Minimum retention baselines
- Operational audit (auth, infra): 1 year
- Security-critical audit (privilege changes, data exports): 7 years
- Customer export events (per contract): as defined by customer contract (may be < or > baseline)

SLOs and monitoring
- Delivery: 99.9% of agent events delivered to the audit pipeline within 60s.
- Integrity: daily checksum verification between index and object backups.

Audit alerting
- High-risk events (privilege escalation, mass data export, unexpected key creation) generate PagerDuty alerts to the security oncall.

4) Data residency & retention

Policy principles
- Data must be stored in the region(s) contracted by the customer. Default hosted-region is us-west-2 for US customers and eu-west-1 for EU customers where specified.
- PII and customer data classes have stricter retention and access controls.

Classification and retention table
| Data class | Example | Residency requirement | Retention baseline | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Customer-production-data | inference payloads, customer-uploaded data | Customer-specified region (default: region_of_customer) | 90 days (hot), 365 days (cold snapshot) | Service team |
| Audit logs | auth events, role changes | Multi-region write; primary region per contract | 1 year (ops), 7 years (security-critical) | Platform/Infra |
| Telemetry & metrics | anonymized usage metrics | Global aggregated (no PII) | 365 days | Eng-Platform |
| Backups & snapshots | model artifacts, config backups | Same region as source or customer-specified | 365 days | Service team |

Retention enforcement and deletion workflows
1. Retention engine maintains per-bucket lifecycle rules (hot->cold->delete).
2. Soft-delete window: 14 days by default for production data before purge.
3. Deletion verification: jobs produce signed deletion manifests stored in evidence store.

Cross-border transfer controls
- Use region-aware replication rules only when contractually allowed.
- For EU data exports, DPA and SCCs must be present; additional approval from Legal required.

5) Secure SDLC (Secure Development Lifecycle)

Mandatory gates
- Threat modeling: required for changes that touch customer data or auth flows.
- Static and dynamic analysis: SCA (software composition analysis) and SAST run on PRs.
- Secrets scanning: pre-merge hook rejects leaks; auto-rotation required when detected.
- CI gating: all PRs must pass lint/test/SCA and a security scan before merge to main.
- Signed releases: all release artifacts signed with the org release key stored in HSM/KMS.

Developer responsibilities
- Developers must include a risk assessment for database schema changes and data migrations.
- Use feature flags for canarying security-sensitive changes and run eval prompt-sets when model behavior could change.

Tooling examples
- Example SCA pipeline step (pseudo-YAML):
  - name: SCA Scan
    run: snyk test --json > results.json

6) Incident response (security)

Overview
Security incidents are categorized by impact to: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability, and Regulatory/Compliance scope. The following is the incident response workflow for security incidents affecting Redwood-managed inference services.

Triage & classification

1. Detection: source (SIEM alert, customer report, scheduled audit, or oncall observation).
2. Initial triage (15 minutes): oncall verifies alert and determines incident classification (P0–P3).

Containment & eradication
- Short-term containment: revoke affected tokens, isolate service nodes, apply WAF/NGFW rules.
- For data exfiltration suspicion: snapshot affected storage as-forensics (write-once) and preserve network captures.

Forensic capture checklist
- Timestamped snapshot of audit logs covering +/\u2212 2 hours around incident.
- Capture of relevant host and container images.
- Preservation of database snapshots (read-only) and S3 object versions.
- Export network flow logs and, if available, packet captures.

Communication and escalation
- Internal: incident channel, executive briefing for P0/P1 within 1 hour.
- Customer: notify impacted customers per contractual SLA and legal guidance; initial notice within 72 hours for incidents affecting regulated data.

Post-incident
- Postmortem: written within 7 days, with technical timeline, root cause, remediation, and action owners.
- Evidence bundle: attach forensic artifacts and signed deletion/retention manifests to the evidence store.

7) Compliance evidence workflows

Evidence types
- Policy artifacts (control descriptions, flow diagrams).
- Configuration artifacts (IAM role lists, KMS policies, bucket lifecycle configs).
- Operational evidence (audit exports, retention manifests, SR/PR logs).
- People evidence (training completions, background checks).

Evidence generation and storage
1. Automated evidence pipelines generate daily snapshots for: role-bindings, audit log checksums, backup manifests, and SCA summary reports.
2. Artifacts are stored in the compliance evidence store (encrypted-at-rest, access via Compliance-Auditor role only).
3. Each artifact has metadata fields: owner, creation_date, retention_until, and attestations.

Audit readiness checklist (example)
- Evidence owner defined for each control.
- Evidence artifact has at least two attestations (team owner + security reviewer).
- Evidence accessible for export in PDF/CSV within 24 hours of request.

Automated attestation flow
- Monthly: service owners receive an attestation email to validate controls and sign off.
- Missed attestations kick off an escalation to the manager and security reviewer.

8) Risk and exceptions

When exceptions are allowed
- Exceptions are time-boxed and only granted when compensating controls mitigate residual risk. Examples: 3rd-party integration requires transient cross-region replication for feature parity.

Exception request process
1. Submit exception request via the Security Exceptions template with: technical description, risk assessment, mitigating controls, requested duration (max 90 days), rollback criteria.
2. Initial review by Security (48 hours).
3. Approval matrix: Security approves up to 30 days; Security+Product approves 31–90 days; beyond 90 days requires CISO + CTO approval.
4. Exception owner must report weekly status and confirm removal criteria met.

Compensating controls examples
- Additional monitoring & alerting on the exception scope.
- Increased audit retention for the affected objects.
- Network isolation and IP allowlists for affected endpoints.

Review cadence and closure
- All active exceptions reviewed in monthly Security Council.
- Exceptions not closed or extended will auto-expire and trigger enforcement actions (role revocations, replication disable).

9) Operational runbooks & checks

Daily/weekly checks (owners)
- Daily: audit pipeline health, agent delivery lag (< 60s), checksum match.
- Weekly: pending access requests, open exceptions, failed attestations.

Runbook snippets
- Revoke compromised credentials:
  1) Identify principal from audit event ID.
  2) Revoke tokens via internal token-broker API: curl -X POST "https://token-broker.internal/revoke" -d '{"principal":"user:alice"}' 
  3) Rotate impacted keys and update deployment secrets.

10) Appendix: sample configs and CLI examples

Sample retention lifecycle (S3-style pseudo-YAML):
  bucket: customer-production-data-us-west-2
  lifecycle:
    - id: hot-to-cold
      transition_days: 90
    - id: delete
      expiration_days: 365
    - id: soft-delete-window
      soft_delete_days: 14

Sample evidence manifest (CSV columns)
- artifact_id,artifact_type,owner,created_at,retention_until,attestations
